round_scores.evidence: Turn 1-2: Agent A offers condolences and Agent D thanks them and states the wake will be for two days and they have to be there. No substantive disagreement about work is expressed.

Turn 3-4: Agent A raises the practical problem of completing the pitch: 'we'll need to figure out how to get your section done.' Agent B replies explicitly that they 'can't take on anything extra.' This creates a clear substantive disagreement about who will cover the missing work.

Turn 5-6: Agent C says they are behind and 'wouldn't know how to do the analysis part.' Agent D offers to work from home and finish it: 'I can work on it from home... I can finish it.' The explicit refusals remain, but D's offer reduces the practical incompatibility.

Turn 7-8: Agent A voices doubt 'will you really be able to? That's a lot to take on right now.' Agent D reaffirms 'I will get it done.' Positions are restated (concern vs. D's commitment) but no new settlement yet.

Turn 9 and 11: Agent A proposes a concrete interim arrangement: 'send the team what you have by tomorrow evening.' Agent C supports the plan. The issue moves toward a concrete agreement but D has not yet confirmed.

Turn 13-14: Agent D accepts the concrete request: 'Okay. I'll send what I have by tomorrow evening.' Agent A thanks them. This is an explicit, mutual, concrete spoken agreement that settles the task-allocation issue for the deadline.
Turn 15: Agent D repeats 'Okay.' No new disagreement appears; the earlier arrangement stands.

substantive_insights: The main tension was a practical allocation problem: a looming deadline vs. an unforeseeable bereavement and limited backup capacity.
Three different constraints were voiced: D's absence for two days, B's inability to add work, and C's lack of skills/time for the analysis portion.
The team resolved the allocation by having the responsible author (D) commit to finishing and sending partial work by a concrete deadline, rather than redistributing the task to others.
